strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: how to combine heterogeneous open-source LLMs through instance-level routing and aggregation, with clear motivation for scalable multi-agent collaboration.

The proposed SMACS framework is conceptually coherent, combining retrieval-based prior model selection with posterior aggregation/ranking, and the paper gives enough high-level detail to understand the main pipeline.

The evaluation spans eight diverse benchmarks covering math, coding, instruction following, medical QA, and general reasoning, and compares against individual open-source models, closed-source APIs, and several multi-model collaboration baselines.

The ablation study supports that the main components contribute incrementally, especially retrieval-based prior selection; additional analyses of scaling, retrieved support-question sources, and aggregator choice are useful.
The appendix lists model bank, dataset splits, prompts, and most hyperparameters, which improves reproducibility relative to many multi-agent LLM papers.
weaknesses: The central claim that open-source collaboration beats leading closed-source LLMs is not fully convincing. The closed-source baselines appear unusually weak on several benchmarks, and the paper does not provide enough detail about API prompting, decoding, evaluation dates, number of samples, or whether baselines were tuned comparably.

The method is very expensive: each test query uses seven referencer LLM calls plus multiple aggregator calls, and adding a new model requires evaluating it over the entire question bank. The scalability claim is therefore mostly about accuracy with more models, not practical compute, latency, or cost scalability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The abstract says code will be released but no repository is given, evaluation scripts are not specified, seeds/variance are absent, and closed-source model results are difficult to independently reproduce.

The experimental design risks overstating generalization: the unified question bank is built from validation splits of the same benchmark families used for testing, so the router may benefit from benchmark-specific nearest-neighbor structure rather than demonstrating robust routing to genuinely new task distributions.

Several methodological choices are underjustified or unclear, including the PPL scorer/model, the scale compatibility of similarity and perplexity in the hybrid posterior score, the sampling/drop procedure, and why a single fixed aggregator is fair across all tasks.

No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run stability are reported despite stochastic sampling, multiple aggregation calls, and small test sets such as AIME, making some reported gains hard to interpret.

The novelty is moderate: the paper combines known ingredients from retrieval-based routing, mixture-of-agents, self-consistency, and best-of-n style selection. The contribution is useful but not clearly a major conceptual advance.

Writing and presentation have polish issues, including grammatical errors, malformed extracted figure/table text, inconsistent terminology such as close-source/closed-source, and an incomplete code-release sentence in the abstract.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem for NLP: how to combine heterogeneous open-source LLMs through instance-level routing and aggregation, rather than relying on a single model.
The proposed system is easy to understand at a high level, combining a retrieval-based prior over model performance with posterior aggregation and reranking.

The evaluation covers a reasonably broad set of benchmarks spanning math, code, instruction following, medicine, and general reasoning, and includes comparisons to individual open-source models and several multi-model baselines.
The paper includes useful ablations of the main components and reports implementation details such as model pool, prompts, hyperparameters, and validation/test splits.
weaknesses: The central claim that open-source collaboration 'beats closed-source LLMs' is not adequately supported because the comparison is not cost-, latency-, or compute-matched. SMACS invokes multiple 20B-72B models plus repeated aggregation/reranking, while the closed-source baselines appear to be single-model calls. This makes the headline claim potentially misleading.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code will be released but gives no repository, and the paper relies on many large models, stochastic decoding, benchmark-specific evaluation scripts, closed-model outputs, and a precomputed question bank/performance matrix that are not made available.

The evaluation methodology lacks statistical rigor. Results are reported as point estimates with no confidence intervals, no repeated-run variance despite temperature 0.7 sampling, and no significance testing. Several reported gains over strong baselines are small on some datasets and may not be robust.

The retrieval question bank is constructed from validation sets of the same benchmark families used for testing, which may make the router strongly benchmark-adapted. The paper does not convincingly test transfer to genuinely unseen tasks or distributions, despite claiming general scalability and generalization.

The closed-source baseline setup is under-specified: API versions, prompts, decoding settings, dates, answer extraction procedures, and whether the authors re-ran or copied results are not sufficiently detailed to support fair comparison.

The method is largely an engineering combination of known ideas: model routing, retrieval over validation examples, mixture-of-agents aggregation, repeated sampling, and reranking by similarity/perplexity. The novelty over existing routing and multi-agent aggregation methods is incremental.

Some technical definitions are unclear or questionable. The perplexity score is written as 1 - PPL without normalization, making its scale incompatible with cosine similarity unless further processing is used; the prior-drop sampling description is also confusing about whether high-prior or low-prior responses are dropped or retained.

The scalability claim is only demonstrated up to 15 models and without reporting computational cost. Since the method requires evaluating every candidate model on the question bank and then querying multiple models per test instance, scalability in practice is not established.

The paper contains clarity and polish issues, including grammatical errors, awkward notation, incomplete code-release placeholder text, and poorly rendered/extracted figures/tables, which reduce confidence in the care of the empirical reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP problem: how to combine heterogeneous open-source LLMs into a scalable multi-agent inference system that can compete with stronger proprietary systems.

The proposed SMACS framework is technically coherent and easy to understand: retrieval-based prior model selection is paired with posterior aggregation, dropping, and reranking, giving a sensible prior/posterior decomposition of the collaboration problem.

The empirical scope is broad, covering eight benchmarks across math, coding, instruction following, medical QA, and general reasoning, with comparisons against individual open-source models, closed-source APIs, and several multi-agent baselines.

The reported results are consistently strong. SMACS improves over the best average open-source and closed-source baselines, and the component ablations support that RPS, similarity scoring, perplexity scoring, and prior-based dropping each contribute some gain.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, including the model bank, prompts, hyperparameters, validation/test splits, inference settings, and aggregator selection analysis, which helps make the work more reproducible than many LLM ensemble papers.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are overstated. Phrases such as “pushing the upper bound of intelligence” and “open-source LLMs collaboration beats closed-source LLMs” are not fully justified, since the comparison is task-set-specific, compute-heavy, and depends on a curated pool of strong models plus repeated aggregation.

The methodology risks benchmark-specific routing advantages: the unified question bank is built from validation portions of the same benchmark families used for testing. Although splits are non-overlapping, this setting may overestimate generalization to genuinely unseen tasks or domains.

The comparison to closed-source models is not entirely clean. Proprietary model results may depend on API version, prompting, sampling, output budget, and evaluation date, and the paper does not provide enough detail to guarantee exact reproducibility of those baselines.

Efficiency is a major practical concern. SMACS invokes multiple 20B-72B models plus repeated aggregation and reranking, but the paper does not provide latency, token, memory, or cost comparisons. This weakens the practical interpretation of gains over single closed-source systems.

The contribution is empirically useful but conceptually somewhat incremental: retrieval-based routing, model ensembling, response aggregation, self-consistency-like sampling, and perplexity/similarity reranking are all established ingredients. The novelty lies mainly in their integration and scale.

Some evaluations have high variance or limited statistical treatment. For example, AIME2024 is small, and the paper reports point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis over random seeds and sampling stochasticity.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: the abstract says “Code will be released at” without a URL, and exact outputs from many large models/API baselines would be difficult to reproduce without released generations, evaluation scripts, and model-serving details.

The paper would be stronger with analysis of failure cases, disagreement patterns, when aggregation hurts, and whether improvements come from true complementary reasoning versus selecting the strongest validation-matched specialist.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely NLP problem: how to orchestrate heterogeneous open-source LLMs through instance-level routing and response aggregation.
The proposed system is clearly decomposed into prior model selection and posterior response enhancement, and the overall idea is plausible and practically motivated.

The empirical section is broad, covering eight benchmarks across math, coding, instruction following, medical QA, and general reasoning, with comparisons to single open-source models, closed-source APIs, and several multi-LLM baselines.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, including model pool composition, prompts, hyperparameters, additional OOD experiments, ablations, cost/latency analysis, and repeated-run statistics on several datasets.
The ablation studies suggest that retrieval-based prior selection and posterior scoring each contribute incremental gains, rather than all improvement coming from a single hidden component.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated. Statements such as surpassing closed-source LLMs and breaking the open-source upper bound conflate an expensive multi-call ensemble with single-model baselines, making the comparison less direct than the headline suggests.

The novelty is moderate: the system combines retrieval-based routing, model ensembling, repeated aggregation, and heuristic final selection. These are reasonable design choices, but the conceptual advance over existing router-plus-aggregation systems is incremental.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL in the abstract and by reliance on many large models, API baselines, and benchmark-specific prompts. The paper gives many details, but reproducing the exact results would still be difficult without released scripts, model-serving setup, and exact evaluation code.

The question-bank setup raises fairness and generalization concerns. The method uses labeled validation data from the same benchmark families used for testing, so part of the gain may come from benchmark-specific model profiling rather than a generally scalable collaboration mechanism.

The scalability claim is only partially supported. Adding a new LLM requires evaluating it over the whole question bank, and inference still uses multiple referencer calls plus multiple aggregation calls. This is scalable in a modular engineering sense, but not clearly scalable in compute or deployment cost.

The posterior scoring heuristic is under-justified. Mean pairwise similarity may reward consensus even when the consensus is wrong, and perplexity as defined and used is not well motivated as a correctness signal. The paper provides empirical PPL ranges but not a strong validation that this score reliably selects better answers.

Some comparisons may be unfair or insufficiently controlled: different systems may use different numbers of calls, aggregation opportunities, context lengths, or best-on-validation choices, and the paper does not fully isolate these factors.

The writing is generally understandable but contains repeated grammar issues, formatting/extraction problems in figures/tables, and occasional imprecise terminology that makes some methodological details harder to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: scalable orchestration of heterogeneous open-source LLMs for task-level and instance-level collaboration.
The proposed system is conceptually simple and plausible, combining retrieval-based prior model selection with posterior aggregation and candidate selection.
The evaluation spans several widely used benchmark families, including math, coding, instruction following, general reasoning, and medical QA.
The paper includes useful ablations, scaling curves, cost/latency estimates, OOD experiments, and prompt details, which help clarify how the system behaves beyond the main table.
Empirically, the reported gains over MoA, self-consistency, Symbolic-MoE, and individual open-source models are often substantial, especially on LiveCodeBench, MMLU-Pro, and AIME.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not yet sufficiently trustworthy for a clear Findings recommendation. The unified question bank is built from validation splits of the same benchmark families used for testing, so much of the gain may come from benchmark-specific routing rather than general scalable collaboration. The OOD evidence is limited and does not fully address this concern.

The paper makes strong claims about surpassing closed-source LLMs, but the comparison is not very fair or well controlled: SMCS uses many open-source model calls plus repeated aggregation, while closed-source baselines appear to be single-call systems. The cost and latency accounting is also underspecified, especially for locally hosted open-source models.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says the code is released but no URL appears, and reproducing the work requires many large models, exact benchmark splits, model outputs over the question bank, scoring scripts, and cost assumptions that are not fully specified.

Several methodological details are ambiguous or underjustified. It is unclear which model computes perplexity, how answer correctness is normalized across free-form tasks, how stochastic sampling variance affects all results, and whether the prior-drop sampling actually drops low-prior or high-prior responses as intended.

The method is an incremental composition of existing ideas: retrieval-based routing, model ensembling, MoA-style aggregation, self-consistency-like repeated sampling, and heuristic candidate scoring. The novelty is mostly in packaging and empirical scaling rather than a clearly new algorithmic insight.

Some evaluation choices raise concern: MATH-500 versus sampled MATH validation may risk overlap or distribution tuning; LiveCodeBench v6 is used as validation while v5 is used as test, which is temporally odd; closed-source numbers may depend heavily on prompt and generation settings; and only four datasets receive repeated-run statistics.

The paper’s presentation has many polish issues, including malformed extracted text/figures, awkward phrasing, inconsistent terminology, and occasional numerical/formatting inconsistencies. These issues do not alone invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in careful experimental execution.

The analysis does not convincingly isolate why SMCS works. The ablations show positive contributions, but the gains from retrieval, aggregation, perplexity, similarity, and the strong fixed aggregator are not disentangled enough to establish the claimed scalability mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely NLP problem: scaling multi-LLM collaboration as new models and tasks are added. The proposed SMCS framework is well aligned with current practical needs around model routing, ensembling, and open-source LLM orchestration.

The method is conceptually sensible: retrieval-based prior selection uses instance-level historical performance from a question bank, while posterior enhancement uses multiple aggregations plus a hybrid selection score. This combination is a reasonable advance over using only a router or only response aggregation.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally strong, covering eight benchmarks across math, coding, instruction following, medicine, and general reasoning, with comparisons to closed-source models, individual open-source models, and several multi-LLM collaboration baselines.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main table, including scaling with number of LLMs, OOD question-bank experiments, prior-selection ranking analysis, posterior-enhancement analysis, component ablations, cost/latency measurements, and repeated-run statistics on several datasets.

The results are practically impressive: SMCS improves average accuracy over strong multi-LLM baselines and often exceeds the best individual open-source model on the evaluated tasks, suggesting that the system is more than a trivial aggregation of many calls.

Implementation details such as the LLM bank, inference settings, hyperparameters, prompts, and validation/test splits are described in enough detail to make the high-level experimental setup understandable.
weaknesses: The central performance claims are somewhat overstated. Comparing a multi-model system with access to benchmark-specific validation banks against single closed-source LLMs is informative, but it is not a clean claim that open-source collaboration generally surpasses those models. The conclusion should more carefully qualify the compute, model-access, and benchmark-adaptation advantages of SMCS.

The unified question bank is constructed from validation splits of the same benchmark families used for testing. Although the test sets are non-overlapping, this gives the method distribution-specific prior information. The OOD experiments help, but the strongest results still rely on same-benchmark support, which limits confidence in broad generalization claims.

Reproducibility remains challenging. The system requires 15 large open-source LLMs, VLLM inference, large context/output budgets, repeated aggregation, and possibly substantial compute. The abstract says code is released but the URL appears missing, and it is unclear whether cached model outputs, question-bank predictions, and exact splits will be released.

Some methodological details are ambiguous or potentially inconsistent. The prior-drop distribution appears to assign higher sampling mass to higher-prior models while the text says inferior references are dropped; the paper should clarify whether the distribution samples retained or discarded references. The perplexity score is also only lightly justified and may be sensitive to model/tokenization choices.

The novelty is useful but mostly compositional. Retrieval over validation examples for routing and multi-response aggregation are both established ideas; the contribution is a strong engineering synthesis rather than a fundamentally new learning or inference principle.

The baseline comparisons could be more rigorous. Some baselines appear adapted with the authors' chosen aggregator and settings, but it is not always clear whether each baseline is equally tuned for cost, number of calls, output budget, prompts, and model pool. This matters because the reported margins are partly driven by orchestration choices.

The paper relies heavily on average accuracy across heterogeneous benchmarks. This average can obscure task-specific tradeoffs, including cases where SMCS ties or underperforms GPT-o3-mini/GPT-4.1 or the open-source upper bound. The main claims would be stronger with more cautious interpretation of these mixed per-task results.

Several clarity issues remain, including grammatical errors, dense figures, and imprecise wording around scalability and performance frontiers. These do not undermine the work, but they reduce polish for main-conference acceptance.
